TAB: On one parsing, ghayr is an adjective of alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a specific proper-name-like definite, so an indefinite adjective can describe it. TAB: The possible accusative parse treats ghayr as a detached adjective of the pronoun in ʿalayhim, which is syntactically governed by anʿamta. TAB-FULL: The first genitive parse makes ghayr an adjective for alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a fully specified proper name but indefinite-like, so it can take this adjective. TAB-FULL: Even if ghayr repeats ṣirāṭ rather than qualifying those favored, their evident description as guided by God already implies they are neither objects of His anger nor astray. TAB-FULL: An accusative reading of ghayr is grammatically possible but al-Ṭabarī dislikes it because it departs from the established, widely transmitted reading; it would qualify the object pronoun in عليهم and mean not objects of anger or misguidance. TAB-FULL: He prefers the universally transmitted genitive reading, taking ghayr as an adjective of those favored or as repeated ṣirāṭ; either parse is sound, and he explains the grammatical alternatives because they produce different interpretations. IBNMUJAHID reporting نافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي: These readers take غير المغضوب عليهم in the genitive as an adjective of الذين; Ibn Kathīr is reported with a different form, though another transmission agrees with the majority. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: As an adjective, ghayr can modify alladhīna here only because the relative phrase does not single out a particular group, making it like an indefinite description. BAYDAWI-FULL reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr reads غير in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier or by an implied verb, and it can also be an exception if favors include both groups. NASAFI-FULL: Alternatively, the phrase qualifies the favored, who combine the full blessing of faith with safety from divine anger and error; the source explains why “other than” can qualify a definite antecedent. ABUHAYYAN: The suggestion that الذين denotes a generic class, allowing ghayr to modify it despite definiteness, undermines the rule that a definite noun is modified only by a definite; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this account. ABUHAYYAN reporting المهدوي: Al-Mahdawī and others parse accusative ghayr as a circumstantial accusative from عليهم, or from الذين; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the latter because the genitive complement has no syntactic position for a circumstantial modifier. SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr can function like illā for exception, as an adjective by analogy with illā, or like lā for negation, permitting its governed object to precede it. BIQAI: Ghayr is made definite by annexation to its opposite and serves as an adjective for those who were blessed, like motion being other than rest. ITQAN: غير is an annexed, indefinite noun; it becomes definite only between two opposites, which permits it to modify the definite phrase “those who incurred anger,” though it usually modifies an indefinite. ABUHAYYAN reporting أبو علي: Abū ʿAlī parses genitive ghayr as an apposition either to الذين or to the pronoun in عليهم; Abū Ḥayyān calls both analyses weak because apposition by an adjective is weak. ABUHAYYAN: Some supply an omitted صراط before ghayr; Abū Ḥayyān finds the estimate weak because it creates awkward apposition or adjective order and other difficult attachment analyses.
